passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — peremptory norms of general international law from which no derogation is permitted — has long occupied an uneasy position in the hierarchy of international legal obligations. Unlike ordinary treaty obligations, which bind only consenting states and may be modified by subsequent agreement, jus cogens norms purport to bind all states regardless of consent, rendering void any treaty or custom inconsistent with them. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties codified this principle in 1969, but the Convention conspicuously declined to enumerate which norms qualify as peremptory, leaving the determination to evolving state practice and the judgments of international tribunals. The result has been a doctrine whose procedural architecture is more assured than its substantive content.

The difficulties that attend any effort to identify peremptory norms are considerable. Proponents of a positivist methodology insist that jus cogens must be derived from near-universal state practice accompanied by opinio juris — the conviction that the practice is legally obligatory — a standard that, rigorously applied, admits very few candidates. The prohibition on torture, the prohibition on genocide, and the rule against slavery command near-universal acceptance and are routinely cited as paradigm cases. Yet even these paradigms are contested at the margins: the permissibility of "enhanced interrogation" by states invoking national-security exceptions illustrates how a norm nominally accepted in the abstract may be systematically evaded in practice without triggering the formal machinery of derogation. Natural-law theorists respond that the positivist criterion is circular: a norm cannot derive its peremptory character from the practice of the very states it is meant to constrain. For this reason, natural-law accounts tend to ground jus cogens in considerations of human dignity that transcend positive law, though critics rightly observe that this approach offers no principled method for distinguishing genuine peremptory norms from the moral preferences of particular legal cultures.

The practical consequences of recognizing a norm as jus cogens extend well beyond the invalidation of conflicting treaties. Under the lex specialis principle, a more specific international rule ordinarily displaces a general one in cases of conflict; jus cogens, however, operates as a lex superior that displaces even lex specialis arrangements. A bilateral investment treaty that would insulate a state's expropriation of indigenous land from international review, for example, might be voided insofar as it conflicts with a peremptory norm prohibiting cultural genocide. Whether such voidance operates automatically or requires a declaratory judgment by a competent tribunal remains contested; the International Court of Justice has thus far avoided a definitive ruling on the point. Furthermore, jus cogens has been invoked to override state immunity in domestic tort proceedings brought by victims of foreign state-sponsored torture, with some national courts accepting the argument and others rejecting it on the ground that customary immunity rules are themselves of longstanding standing and cannot be displaced without clearer international consensus.

The normative incoherence of jus cogens — simultaneously the most authoritative tier of international law and the least precisely defined — has prompted some scholars to recommend confining the doctrine to a narrow, enumerated list subject to formal amendment procedures analogous to those governing constitutional revision. This proposal has considerable appeal: it would restore the rule-of-law values of predictability and equal treatment that jus cogens, in its current open-textured form, conspicuously lacks. Yet the recommendation risks calcifying norms at a particular historical moment and foreclosing the incremental evolution through which international law has historically accommodated moral progress. One hopes that international tribunals, rather than national courts acting in isolation, will assume the principal responsibility for articulating jus cogens with the rigor and consistency that its foundational ambitions demand.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens is fundamentally incompatible with the positivist methodology that underlies most international treaty law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although jus cogens occupies the highest tier of international legal obligation, its practical effectiveness is undermined by states that invoke national-security exceptions to evade compliance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jus cogens is a doctrine whose procedural status in international law is well established but whose substantive content and practical application remain deeply uncertain, a problem that international tribunals are best positioned to address.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's failure to enumerate peremptory norms has rendered jus cogens largely unenforceable as a matter of positive international law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proposals to codify jus cogens through formal amendment procedures would best reconcile the doctrine's foundational ambitions with the rule-of-law values of predictability and equal treatment.

explanations.correct: The passage consistently argues that jus cogens has a secure formal status (codified in the Vienna Convention, acknowledged as lex superior) but that its substantive content is poorly defined and its application inconsistent — and closes by urging international tribunals to take the lead in resolving this. C integrates both strands and captures the author's closing prescription.
explanations.A: Too narrow and misstates the argument. The passage does not claim jus cogens is incompatible with positivism; it describes a methodological debate between positivists and natural-law theorists without endorsing either.
explanations.B: Paragraph-level restatement of one portion of paragraph two. It omits the structural tension between procedural clarity and substantive uncertainty that organizes the entire passage.
explanations.D: Overstates the consequence. The author says the lack of enumeration leaves determination to evolving practice, not that the doctrine is unenforceable.
explanations.E: Restates a suggestion discussed at the end of paragraph four as the main point. The author presents this proposal but immediately qualifies it, making it one consideration rather than the thesis.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its formal codification described; two competing methodologies for identifying its content are assessed; its practical legal consequences are examined; and a reform proposal is evaluated with a qualified endorsement of a preferred institutional solution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal controversy is introduced; historical evidence for one side is marshaled; the opposing side's evidence is dismissed as insufficient; and the author's preferred position is defended.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrine is defined; its origins in natural law are traced; its positivist critique is refuted; and a proposal for replacing it with a more workable framework is advanced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced; its historical development across three eras is surveyed; its contemporary application is illustrated with two cases; and scholars' reactions to those cases are summarized.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A doctrine's formal status is contrasted with a rival doctrine; the practical advantages of each are compared; a synthesis of the two is proposed; and the synthesis is tested against a hypothetical case.

explanations.correct: Paragraph one introduces jus cogens and notes the gap between its procedural architecture and substantive content. Paragraph two examines positivist and natural-law methodologies for identifying the norms. Paragraph three surveys practical legal consequences (lex specialis displacement, state immunity). Paragraph four assesses the codification proposal and ends with a qualified prescription favoring international tribunals. A tracks these four moves accurately.
explanations.B: Mis-characterizes the structure. The passage does not marshal evidence for one side and dismiss the other; both positivist and natural-law accounts are found wanting, and the author's closing preference is institutional (tribunals), not doctrinal.
explanations.C: Wrong in two respects: the passage does not trace jus cogens to natural law as a matter of origin, and the positivist critique is not refuted — it is described as facing its own objections.
explanations.D: The passage does not survey three historical eras; its structure is analytical rather than chronological.
explanations.E: There is no rival doctrine being contrasted as a whole, and no synthesis is proposed. This description misidentifies the genre of the passage.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties did which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It enumerated an authoritative list of norms qualifying as jus cogens and assigned to the International Court of Justice the task of enforcing them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It codified the principle that peremptory norms bind all states regardless of consent while leaving the identification of specific norms to state practice and tribunal judgments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It established a formal amendment procedure by which states could collectively modify or derogate from peremptory norms over time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It recognized jus cogens as binding only on states that had ratified the Convention, thereby preserving the consent-based architecture of treaty law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It superseded earlier customary international law on state immunity by declaring torture and genocide to be automatically void under the lex specialis principle.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that the Vienna Convention 'codified this principle in 1969, but the Convention conspicuously declined to enumerate which norms qualify as peremptory, leaving the determination to evolving state practice and the judgments of international tribunals.' B paraphrases this precisely.
explanations.A: Contradicts the passage directly. The Convention declined to enumerate norms and did not assign enforcement to the ICJ.
explanations.C: The passage mentions an amendment-procedure analogy only as a scholar's proposal; the Convention itself is not described as establishing such a procedure.
explanations.D: Inverts the passage's claim. Jus cogens binds all states regardless of consent, which is what distinguishes it from ordinary treaty obligations.
explanations.E: The passage distinguishes jus cogens from lex specialis, explaining that jus cogens operates as lex superior over lex specialis. It does not describe the Vienna Convention as superseding immunity norms via lex specialis.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about the positivist methodology for identifying jus cogens norms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It should be abandoned entirely in favor of a natural-law approach grounded in universal human dignity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When applied rigorously, it would recognize a far smaller number of peremptory norms than most international lawyers currently accept.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is superior to natural-law approaches because it provides a principled method for distinguishing peremptory norms from culturally contingent moral preferences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its requirement of near-universal state practice is rendered wholly unworkable by states that systematically evade their treaty obligations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the methodology tacitly endorsed by the Vienna Convention, which grounded jus cogens in the consent of the international community.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the positivist standard, 'rigorously applied, admits very few candidates,' implying that a strict positivist analysis would recognize far fewer peremptory norms than is conventional. B is a careful paraphrase of this claim.
explanations.A: The author does not endorse natural law as a replacement. The passage explicitly notes that natural-law accounts 'offer no principled method for distinguishing genuine peremptory norms from the moral preferences of particular legal cultures,' a criticism the author presents without rebuttal.
explanations.C: The passage identifies circularity as a problem with positivism and does not characterize it as superior to natural law. Both approaches are presented as flawed.
explanations.D: Overstates the passage. The author says states evade norms by invoking exceptions 'without triggering the formal machinery of derogation,' but does not conclude that the positivist criterion is wholly unworkable because of this.
explanations.E: The passage does not characterize the Vienna Convention as endorsing positivism. The Convention's silence on enumeration is a procedural feature, not a methodological commitment.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of a bilateral investment treaty that insulates a state's expropriation of indigenous land from international review (paragraph 3) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the practical consequence that jus cogens, as a lex superior, can void specific treaty arrangements that conflict with peremptory norms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: establish that investment treaties are the category of international agreement most frequently invalidated by peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that the prohibition on cultural genocide is among the best-established and least-contested peremptory norms in international law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the approach of international tribunals with that of domestic courts in resolving disputes over indigenous land rights.

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide evidence that the lex specialis principle has been effectively displaced by jus cogens in all areas of international economic law.

explanations.correct: The example is introduced immediately after the claim that jus cogens operates as a lex superior displacing even lex specialis arrangements. The bilateral investment treaty example concretizes exactly this legal consequence — how a specific treaty could be voided by a conflicting peremptory norm. A correctly identifies the illustrative function.
explanations.B: The passage does not claim investment treaties are the most frequently invalidated category; the example is illustrative, not taxonomic.
explanations.C: The passage frames the example hypothetically ('might be voided'), which suggests the prohibition's application here is contested, not well-established. The function is not to certify the norm's status.
explanations.D: The contrast between international tribunals and domestic courts is addressed separately in the same paragraph regarding state immunity; it is not the function of the investment-treaty example.
explanations.E: The passage says jus cogens displaces lex specialis in cases of conflict, not that it has displaced it 'in all areas of international economic law.' This answer overgeneralizes.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the proposal to confine jus cogens to a narrow, enumerated list subject to formal amendment procedures can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, because it would restore predictability and equal treatment to an area of law currently lacking both.

choices.label: B
choices.text: unconditional rejection, because it would calcify norms and prevent international law from accommodating moral progress.

choices.label: C
choices.text: qualified appreciation tempered by concern that codification risks foreclosing the incremental evolution through which international law has historically developed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutrally descriptive presentation of a scholarly debate without any evaluative stance by the author.

choices.label: E
choices.text: cautious skepticism rooted primarily in the view that the amendment procedures proposed are modeled too closely on constitutional revision to be workable in an international context.

explanations.correct: The author grants the proposal 'considerable appeal' and acknowledges it would restore rule-of-law values, but immediately qualifies this: it 'risks calcifying norms at a particular historical moment and foreclosing the incremental evolution' through which international law develops. This is a paradigm case of qualified appreciation — recognizing merit while identifying a significant risk.
explanations.A: Overstates the positivity. The author describes the appeal but does not endorse the proposal; the qualification is substantive, not perfunctory.
explanations.B: Overstates the negativity. The author does not reject the proposal unconditionally; the passage opens with praise ('considerable appeal') before entering the qualification.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The author explicitly editorializes — 'considerable appeal,' the risk of 'calcifying,' and the closing prescription to favor international tribunals all reflect an evaluative stance.
explanations.E: The author does not raise workability concerns about the amendment-procedure analogy. The concern is about foreclosing moral evolution, not about the mechanics of the proposed procedure.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the natural-law theorists' response to the positivist methodology as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The states that most consistently comply with jus cogens prohibitions are also those with the strongest domestic constitutional traditions of human-dignity protection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several international tribunals have relied on the positivist criterion of state practice and opinio juris to confirm that the prohibition on torture qualifies as a peremptory norm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A comparative survey of major legal systems reveals that the concept of human dignity is understood in substantially different ways across cultures, with no consensus on its minimum content.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's drafters included a provision stating that jus cogens derives its authority from the consent of states, not from any pre-legal moral order.

choices.label: E
choices.text: States that invoke national-security exceptions to torture prohibitions frequently face diplomatic sanctions from other states, indicating that such evasions are not widely accepted.

explanations.correct: The natural-law theorists' response is that jus cogens should be grounded in considerations of human dignity that transcend positive law. The objection the author already notes is that this approach 'offers no principled method for distinguishing genuine peremptory norms from the moral preferences of particular legal cultures.' If human dignity is understood in substantially different ways across cultures with no consensus on its minimum content, this directly undermines the claim that human dignity can serve as a trans-positive foundation for jus cogens — it would show that the natural-law anchor is itself culturally contingent.
explanations.A: This would, if anything, lend support to natural-law theorists by suggesting a link between domestic human-dignity traditions and international compliance; it does not undermine their position.
explanations.B: This addresses the positivist methodology, not the natural-law response to it. It may support positivism but does not undermine natural law's claim about the limitations of positivism.
explanations.D: This would undermine jus cogens generally or support a positivist reading of the Convention, but the natural-law theorists' specific argument is about the normative foundation for peremptory norms — not about what the Convention's drafters intended. The natural-law claim is a philosophical one about what ought to ground jus cogens, not an empirical claim about the Convention's history.
explanations.E: This actually strengthens the positivist account by showing that state practice condemns evasion, and it is irrelevant to the natural-law theorists' separate claim about grounding norms in human dignity.
